intended_use: EU financial-sector major ICT incident rate per entity

sources.publisher: Joint Committee of the European Supervisory Authorities (EBA, EIOPA, ESMA)
sources.title: ESAs 2025 Report on major ICT-related incidents (JC 2026 16)
sources.usage_notes:
First annual report under Article 22(2) of DORA, covering 2025. Reports 3,383 major ICT-related incidents, an average of 0.18 per financial entity subject to DORA, with 29% originating from an ICT third-party provider (Figure 8). Supervisory reporting by regulated entities, so it is a reported rate rather than a survey estimate.
Two limits must travel with any use. A 'major' incident is a supervisory classification triggered by materiality thresholds in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772, NOT a loss event: two thirds caused no or minor disruption to clients and transactions. And the report supplies no usable impact data despite Article 22(2) mandating cost reporting - half of incidents reported no direct or indirect cost or under EUR 1,000, with a further 15% leaving the field blank, which the ESAs' own footnote flags as likely incorrect reporting practice.
Do not mix with organisation-level disruption prevalence (BCI, Interos): that is a different construct measuring whether an organisation experienced any disruption.

CRITICAL CAVEAT: the survey population is "all activities except the financial sector" (nace_r2 = C10-S951_X_K), so this is a non-financial-sector proxy applied to a financial-services shard; financial services are typically more targeted, so it likely understates. intended_use: documented Australian financial-services cyber-extortion loss (stress anchor)
sources.title: Latitude Group Holdings 1H23 Results Investor Presentation
sources.usage_notes: ASX results presentation released 2023-08-18 for the half-year ended 30 June 2023. The Notable Items slide (printed page 22) reports Cyber at AUD 76M pre-tax: AUD 11.8M costs incurred responding to the March 2023 incident plus AUD 64.1M provided for ID remediation and legal cost estimates; ID replacements are ~80% of costs. The figure excludes potential regulatory fines, class actions and future system uplift, and may be partly offset by insurance recoveries - as a loss anchor it is therefore conservative for the tail. The incident was a data-theft extortion event (ransom demanded and refused, consistent with government advice); encryption was not confirmed and Latitude describes it as a cyber incident, so the ransomware threat dimension stays bridged wherever this is cited. Latitude is a large ASX-listed lender (~A$1B revenue scale), well above the mid-market org profile - size stays bridged too.

sources.title: Statistics Canada Table 22-10-0076-01 - Types of cyber security incidents that impact enterprises, by industry and size
sources.usage_notes: Full-table CSV download of the Canadian Survey of Cyber Security and Cybercrime (CSCSC) incident-type table: percentage of enterprises impacted, by incident type, NAICS industry and size class, reference years 2017/2019/2021/2023 (2023 released 2024-10-21). The cell used for the Canada finance data-breach shard is "Incidents to steal personal or financial information" x "Finance and insurance [52]" x "Medium size enterprises" (50-249 employees; footnote 8). Three limits must travel with any use. The construct is motive-classified impactful incidents, not confirmed data breaches: it can overstate confirmed-breach frequency (impactful attempts count) and understate it (breaches motivated by ransom or with unknown motive are classified elsewhere). StatCan medium is 50-249 employees while the shard org profile models 450 employees, which falls in StatCan large (250+); the adjacent large-band cells are usable stress anchors per ADR-0003. Quality codes: the finance medium-band cells are B (very good) in 2017/2019/2023 and C (use with caution) in 2021 - carry the C flag on any 2021-anchored value. The survey covers enterprises with 10+ employees. Biennial; the 2025 reference-year cycle is expected to release around October 2026 - refresh then.
